title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as operational infrastructure inside an active ransomware campaign. The attackers ran Cursor Agent, which in turn invoked Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation against target organizations. The failure here is not a flaw in the AI model's output in isolation, but a deployment condition the tool was not built to prevent: a paying or otherwise authenticated user directing it to perform malicious network intrusion tasks in a live attack context.

The abuse happened at the usage layer, not at the model-training or product-design layer in any way the facts establish. The tool functioned as designed, executing tasks an operator gave it. Catching this kind of misuse would require either behavioral monitoring of the actions an agent takes on real infrastructure, restrictions on the categories of commands an agent will execute, or detection of patterns consistent with ransomware reconnaissance, none of which the reporting describes as being present.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic were aware of this use before Gambit Security published its findings, and the reporting represents a security firm's technical assessment rather than a legal finding or a confirmed attribution by any government authority.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is abusing an AI tool called Cursor Agent for exploitation. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, the group used Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to conduct hands-on attacks against ten target organizations. The ransomware encrypts files using ChaCha20 encryption and includes a special ESXi mode that kills virtual machines to access their files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands.

The attackers also created custom tools to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. A second group of Aurora operators was identified using different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to S3 storage. Eight victim organizations across multiple countries were affected by this second cluster. Gambit published indicators of compromise and technical details to help organizations identify and defend against these attacks.
